power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p = .482", "p ≥ .117", "p ≥ .228" ), Sentence = c("The joint Wald test indicated no significant differences in profile-specific means across T1 and T2, χ²(6) = 5.50, p = .482.", "Age and length of inpatient stay were not significantly associated with profile membership at T1 or with transitions from T1 to T2 (all p ≥ .117; Supplementary Table S1).", "Similarly, the number of attended AAT sessions was not significantly associated with transitions from T1 to T2 (all p ≥ .228)." )), row.names = c(NA, -3L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. text.text: Background and objectives: Adolescents receiving inpatient mental health care differ considerably in their symptom burden, psychological resources, and patterns of change.

This study identified latent profiles based on depressive symptoms and mindfulness and examined transitions between these profiles among adolescents participating in animal-assisted group psychotherapy.

Methods: The sample comprised 108 adolescent inpatients aged 12-18 years (M age = 15.84 years, SD = 1.26) who participated in a five-week animal-assisted group psychotherapy program alongside standard inpatient treatment.
Depressive symptoms and mindfulness were assessed before and after the intervention using the Beck Depression Inventory-Fast Screen and the Freiburg Mindfulness Inventory.
Profiles for each time point were identified using latent profile analysis and linked longitudinally using latent transition analysis.

Results: Three profiles were identified at both measurement points: reduced burden (T1: n = 14, 14.0%; T2: n = 28, 26.7%), characterized by low depressive symptoms and high mindfulness; moderate burden (T1: n = 46, 46.0%; T2: n = 33, 31.4%); and elevated burden (T1: n = 40, 40.0%; T2: n = 44, 41.9%), characterized by high depressive symptoms and low mindfulness.

Estimated transition probabilities indicated that 100% of adolescents in the reduced-burden profile and 86.9% of those in the elevated-burden profile at T1 remained in their respective profiles at T2.
Among adolescents in the moderate-burden profile at T1, 27.7% transitioned to the reduced-burden profile over the five-week intervention period.
Conclusions: Adolescents showed distinct depression-mindfulness profiles with different patterns of stability and change.
Adolescents with moderate initial burden were most likely to transition toward a more favorable profile, suggesting that they may represent a particularly responsive subgroup.
These findings highlight heterogeneity in adolescents' patterns of functioning and change during multimodal inpatient treatment incorporating animal-assisted group psychotherapy.

Research on animal-assisted approaches in youth mental health has examined a range of outcomes, including symptoms of anxiety, depression, trauma-related difficulties, and ADHD, as well as psychological well-being and functioning.

Systematic reviews and meta-analyses suggest potential benefits across these domains, although findings remain mixed and methodological limitations persist (Brandão et al., 2025; Dumouchel & Soubelet, 2026; Hoagwood et al., 2017; Jones et al., 2019; Yu et al., 2025).

text.text: Evidence from psychiatric inpatient settings, however, remains limited and heterogeneous with respect to clinical populations, intervention formats, treatment dose, outcome measures, and study design (Fornefeld et al., 2025).

text.text: Moreover, studies of animal-assisted approaches in youth psychiatric care have primarily examined mean-level pre-post changes, between-group differences, immediate session-related changes, or feasibility and acceptability (Fodstad et al., 2019; Stefanini et al., 2015 Stefanini et al., , 2016)).
text.formatted: Moreover, studies of animal-assisted approaches in youth psychiatric care have primarily examined mean-level pre-post changes, between-group differences, immediate session-related changes, or feasibility and acceptability <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Fodstad et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Stefanini et al., 2015</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Stefanini et al., , 2016))</ref>.

text.text: These approaches provide important information about overall outcomes but offer limited insight into whether adolescents enter treatment with different configurations of symptoms and psychological resources and whether these configurations remain stable or change over time in response to treatment.
Person-centered methods provide a complementary approach for examining such heterogeneity.

Rather than focusing primarily on associations or average differences between variables, person-centered approaches identify subgroups of individuals who show similar patterns across multiple characteristics (Lanza & Rhoades, 2013).
text.formatted: Rather than focusing primarily on associations or average differences between variables, person-centered approaches identify subgroups of individuals who show similar patterns across multiple characteristics <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Lanza & Rhoades, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Latent profile analysis (LPA) can be used to identify unobserved subgroups based on patterns across continuous indicators, whereas latent transition analysis (LTA) extends this approach longitudinally by estimating the probabilities of remaining in the same profile or transitioning to another profile across measurement occasions (Collins & Lanza, 2009; Nylund-Gibson et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Latent profile analysis (LPA) can be used to identify unobserved subgroups based on patterns across continuous indicators, whereas latent transition analysis (LTA) extends this approach longitudinally by estimating the probabilities of remaining in the same profile or transitioning to another profile across measurement occasions <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Collins & Lanza, 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Nylund-Gibson et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: In treatment research, these methods can therefore characterize heterogeneity in functioning at a given time point as well as different patterns of stability and change over a treatment period (Thompson et al., 2011).
text.formatted: In treatment research, these methods can therefore characterize heterogeneity in functioning at a given time point as well as different patterns of stability and change over a treatment period <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Thompson et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Applications in child and adolescent mental health illustrate the potential of this approach.

LPA studies have identified subgroups differing in symptom severity, emotion dysregulation, and transdiagnostic psychological processes, with some evidence that these profiles are associated with subsequent clinical outcomes (Caporino et al., 2016; Evans et al., 2021; Kennedy et al., 2022).
text.formatted: LPA studies have identified subgroups differing in symptom severity, emotion dysregulation, and transdiagnostic psychological processes, with some evidence that these profiles are associated with subsequent clinical outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Caporino et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Evans et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Kennedy et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Longitudinal person-centered analyses can additionally examine how individuals move between profiles.

For example, Melero et al. (2022) identified low-and high-anxiety/depression profiles among children participating in a transdiagnostic prevention program and found that some children transitioned from the higher-to the lower-symptom profile over time.

(2022)</ref> identified low-and high-anxiety/depression profiles among children participating in a transdiagnostic prevention program and found that some children transitioned from the higher-to the lower-symptom profile over time.

text.text: Together, these studies demonstrate how person-centered approaches can complement analyses of average change by describing clinically meaningful heterogeneity and patterns of change within treatment samples.
Depressive symptoms and mindfulness provide useful indicators for examining such heterogeneity among adolescents receiving inpatient mental health care.
Depressive symptoms affect a substantial proportion of adolescents and constitute an important dimension of mental health burden in this age group (Shorey et al., 2022).

text.text: Mindfulness, in contrast, refers to present-moment attention combined with an open and accepting orientation toward ongoing experience (Bishop et al., 2004) and has been associated with several aspects of psychological functioning, including emotion regulation and psychological well-being (Keng et al., 2011).

text.text: Mindfulness may also be conceptually relevant to animal-assisted work because interaction with animals can involve attending to immediate, often nonverbal cues and continuously adapting to the present situation.
Animal-assisted mindfulness approaches have explicitly drawn on this rationale (Schramm et al., 2015).

text.text: Examining depressive symptoms together with mindfulness therefore allows symptom burden and a potentially adaptive psychological resource to be considered simultaneously rather than in isolation.

The present study examined heterogeneity in depressive symptoms and mindfulness among adolescents participating in a five-week animal-assisted group psychotherapy program alongside standard inpatient psychosomatic treatment.

Separate LPAs were used to identify profiles based on depressive symptoms and mindfulness at the beginning and end of the five-week period, and these profiles were subsequently linked longitudinally using LTA to examine profile stability and transitions.
The first aim was to identify latent profiles characterized by different patterns of depressive symptoms and mindfulness at the beginning and end of the five-week period.
The second aim was to examine stability and transitions between these profiles over time.

Based on previous person-centered research in youth mental health, we expected to identify distinct profiles reflecting different combinations of symptom burden and mindfulness (Evans et al., 2021; Kennedy et al., 2022; Melero et al., 2022).

text.text: Given the limited evidence on person-centered patterns of change during AAT, profile stability and transitions were examined without specific directional hypotheses.

By applying a longitudinal person-centered approach, the study aimed to provide a more differentiated understanding of heterogeneity and change during animal-assisted group psychotherapy embedded within adolescent inpatient care.
The data were drawn from a larger clinical study conducted with adolescent inpatients receiving treatment at the Schön Klinik Bad Arolsen, Germany.
The sample initially consisted of 111 patients.
Three patients were excluded because of extensive missing data, resulting in a final analytic sample of 108 adolescents.

Patients were eligible if they were between 12 and 18 years old at the beginning of treatment, had sufficient German language proficiency, had received a diagnosis of a mental health disorder according to the International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems, 10th Revision (ICD-10; World Health Organization, 2004).
text.formatted: Patients were eligible if they were between 12 and 18 years old at the beginning of treatment, had sufficient German language proficiency, had received a diagnosis of a mental health disorder according to the International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems, 10th Revision <ref type="bibr">(ICD-10;</ref> <ref type="bibr">World Health Organization, 2004)</ref>.

text.text: Eligible diagnoses included major depressive episodes, eating disorders, anxiety disorders, and obsessivecompulsive disorder.
Although the registered protocol initially specified an upper age limit of 17 years, this criterion was extended to 18 years to correspond to the age range treated at the clinic.

Exclusion criteria comprised acute suicidality, schizophrenia, schizoaffective disorder, bipolar disorder, substance use disorder, organic mental disorder, a current Axis I disorder other than the primary diagnosis, severe physical illness, reduced physical fitness due to anorexia nervosa, and ongoing therapeutically supervised eating within the clinic among patients with eating disorders.
Additional exclusion criteria for participation in the AAT program were pronounced emotional instability, fear of animals, and allergy to animal hair.
The present study employed a pretest-posttest design, examining adolescents before and after a five-week animal-assisted group psychotherapy program.
The AAT program was offered as part of inpatient psychosomatic care and was intended for patients who were expected to benefit from therapeutic work involving animals.

Goals included promoting mindfulness and self-awareness, strengthening self-esteem and self-efficacy, developing assertiveness and boundary-setting skills, addressing self-image and identity, increasing activation, and supporting treatment engagement.
Patients were referred to AAT by their treating psychotherapists and physicians.
Before enrollment, the clinical team assessed whether each patient was physically and emotionally able to participate safely in group sessions outside the clinic.
Particular attention was given to the physical condition of patients with eating disorders.
Suitability for AAT was determined in consultation with the head physician and/or the responsible ward physician.
The AAT program was provided in addition to the standard multimodal inpatient treatment received by all participants.

Standard inpatient treatment included pharmacotherapy, individual and group psychotherapy, sports therapy, art therapy, supervised group meals, mindfulness-based therapy, and other therapeutic services.
Participants completed questionnaires immediately before the start of the AAT program (T1) and after completion of the five-week intervention period (T2).
Before participation, patients and their legal guardians gave informed consent.
The study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and applicable German legal and regulatory requirements.
The study protocol was reviewed and approved by the legal department of Schön Klinik.
The study was registered in the Dutch Trial Register on March 1, 2021; the registration is currently available through the Research with Human Participants registry.

The intervention was delivered by a child and adolescent psychotherapist in training who was The intervention was intended to use structured human-animal interactions to support emotional stabilization, activation, intrinsic motivation, mindfulness, and self-efficacy.
It consisted of five weekly sessions, each lasting approximately 150 minutes, and was conducted on the therapist's farm.
Groups included no more than seven adolescents.
Each session combined theoretical input, practical exercises involving animals, and guided reflection.

The theoretical material covered topics such as human-animal relationships, mindful awareness, nonverbal communication, body language, emotional expression, personal boundaries, and experiences in relationships.
Practical exercises involved observing, approaching, communicating with, and mindfully guiding dogs and horses.

The therapist provided individualized feedback to help participants recognize how their internal emotional states were communicated through their behavior and how changes in body language affected the interaction.
The sessions increased progressively in complexity over the course of the program.
Initial sessions focused on becoming acquainted with the animals and observing nonverbal communication.
Later sessions addressed mindful leadership, boundaries, relationship patterns, and the transfer of experiences from the animal interactions to everyday situations.
The final session included the application and integration of these skills during a group walk.

text.text: Attendance was documented as the total number of completed sessions.
Dogs, horses, and ponies participated in the intervention.
The program involved six mixedbreed dogs between 4 and 11 years of age.
Four of the dogs belonged to the therapist and lived on the farm, whereas two belonged to another staff member and were present on most intervention days.
The group included three female and three male dogs.
All dogs had been trained by the therapist and evaluated by a veterinarian to determine their suitability for therapeutic work.
Three horses and two Shetland ponies were housed at the farm in a spacious, natural openstable environment.
The horses consisted of an English Warmblood mare, a Zweibrücker mare, and a Haflinger-Quarter Horse cross gelding, ranging in age from 10 to 22 years.
The two Shetland mares were 4 and 5 years old.
A certified animal-welfare practitioner was present throughout the sessions and monitored the animals continuously.
Participation by the animals was voluntary, and each animal could move away from or discontinue an interaction at any point.
Depressive symptoms were assessed before (T1) and after (T2) the intervention using the German version of the Beck Depression Inventory-Fast Screen (BDI-FS; Beck et al., 2000).
text.formatted: Depressive symptoms were assessed before (T1) and after (T2) the intervention using the German version of the Beck Depression Inventory-Fast Screen (BDI-FS; <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Beck et al., 2000)</ref>.

text.text: The BDI-FS comprises seven cognitive and affective items derived from the BDI-II.
Items are rated from 0 to 3, yielding a total score ranging from 0 to 21, with higher scores indicating greater depressive symptom severity.
Scores of 0-3 indicate minimal, 4-8 mild, 9-12 moderate, and 13-21 severe symptoms.
A score of 4 or higher has been proposed as an indicator of clinically relevant symptoms.
In a German population sample, the BDI-FS demonstrated good internal consistency (α = .84) and satisfactory discriminant validity (Kliem et al., 2014).

text.text: Mindfulness was assessed at the beginning (T1) and end (T2) of the intervention using the German version of the Freiburg Mindfulness Inventory (Freiburger Fragebogen zur Achtsamkeit; FFA; Walach et al., 2006).

text.text: The 30-item FFA assesses mindful awareness and acceptance of presentmoment experiences, including attention to current experience, nonjudgmental acceptance, and openness toward internal states.
Items are rated from 1 (rarely) to 4 (almost always) and summed to yield a total score ranging from 30 to 120, with higher scores indicating greater mindfulness.
The 30item version has demonstrated excellent internal consistency (α = .93) and construct validity in meditating and nonmeditating samples (Walach et al., 2006).

text.text: Missing data on the profile indicators were handled using full-information maximum likelihood under the missing-at-random assumption, allowing participants with missing data on one indicator to contribute to model estimation.
Depressive symptoms and mindfulness were used as continuous profile indicators.
The models were estimated using the original, unstandardized BDI-FS and FFA scores, z-standardized values were used only for graphical presentation.
Latent profile models were first estimated separately at T1 and T2.
At each occasion, solutions containing one to five profiles were examined under different variance-covariance parameterizations (Masyn, 2013; Pastor et al., 2007).

text.text: Lower information-criterion values indicated better relative fit, while a significant aLMR-LRT indicated that a k-profile solution provided better fit than the corresponding k -1 profile solution.
Entropy was used to assess classification certainty, with higher values indicating clearer separation between profiles (Celeux & Soromenho, 1996).
text.formatted: Entropy was used to assess classification certainty, with higher values indicating clearer separation between profiles <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Celeux & Soromenho, 1996)</ref>.

text.text: After selecting the best-fitting latent profile solution at both measurement occasions, a longitudinal LTA was estimated using the selected number of profiles at T1 and T2.
The model estimated the probabilities of remaining in the same profile or transitioning to another profile from T1 to T2.
Longitudinal invariance of the profile-specific indicator means was examined to assess whether corresponding profiles had comparable substantive meaning across occasions.
An unrestricted model, in which profile-specific means were estimated freely at T1 and T2, was compared with an invariant model in which corresponding means were constrained to equality across time.
The equality constraints were evaluated using a joint Wald test and by comparing AIC, BIC, and SABIC values.

To examine covariates while accounting for classification uncertainty, we used the manual maximum likelihood three-step approach (Asparouhov & Muthén, 2014; Nylund-Gibson et al., 2014; Vermunt, 2010).
text.formatted: To examine covariates while accounting for classification uncertainty, we used the manual maximum likelihood three-step approach <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Asparouhov & Muthén, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Nylund-Gibson et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Vermunt, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Profile assignments and classification-error probabilities were obtained from the invariant model and incorporated into the subsequent covariate models.
Age and length of inpatient stay were examined as predictors of profile membership at T1 and of transitions from T1 to T2.
Because the number of attended AAT sessions was measured during the intervention, it was examined only as a predictor of transitions from T1 to T2.

Associations between these covariates and initial profile membership and subsequent profile transitions were estimated using multinomial logistic regression and are reported as odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals, with one latent profile serving as the reference category.

The present study used a person-centered approach to examine heterogeneity in depressive symptoms and mindfulness among adolescents participating in animal-assisted group psychotherapy during inpatient psychosomatic treatment.

Three profiles with similar patterns of depressive symptoms and mindfulness were identified at the beginning and end of the five-week period and were characterized by reduced, moderate, and elevated burden.
The moderate-burden profile showed greatest change in response to treatment, primarily toward the reduced-burden profile.
The reducedand elevated-burden profiles however showed high estimated stability and limited response to treatment.
These findings illustrate how longitudinal person-centered analyses can complement mean-level analyses by identifying heterogeneity in patterns of functioning and change within a treatment sample.

The three profiles primarily reflected an ordered pattern of burden: depressive symptoms and mindfulness were inversely patterned across profiles, with higher depressive symptoms accompanied by lower mindfulness and lower depressive symptoms accompanied by higher mindfulness.

This inverse pattern aligns with previous research linking greater mindfulness with fewer internalizing symptoms and more adaptive psychological functioning in adolescents (Keng et al., 2011; Royuela-Colomer et al., 2021).
text.formatted: This inverse pattern aligns with previous research linking greater mindfulness with fewer internalizing symptoms and more adaptive psychological functioning in adolescents <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Keng et al., 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Royuela-Colomer et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, the profiles appeared to represent different levels of overall psychological burden rather than qualitatively distinct combinations of depressive symptoms and mindfulness.

Nevertheless, this finding is consistent with previous person-centered research demonstrating heterogeneity in psychological functioning among children and adolescents receiving psychological interventions (Evans et al., 2021; Kennedy et al., 2022; Melero et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Nevertheless, this finding is consistent with previous person-centered research demonstrating heterogeneity in psychological functioning among children and adolescents receiving psychological interventions <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Evans et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Kennedy et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Melero et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: The transition findings provide a highly relevant and more differentiated picture of change over the five-week period.

Adolescents in the moderate-burden profile showed the greatest variability as illustrated by transitions of 28% of adolescent transitioning to the reduced-burden profile, whereas transitions to the elevated-burden profile were uncommon.

Thus, a subgroup of adolescents who initially showed intermediate levels of depressive symptoms and mindfulness moved toward a more favorable pattern characterized by lower depressive symptoms and higher mindfulness.
One possible explanation is that adolescents with moderate initial burden may have been particularly amenable to change over a relatively brief treatment period.

They had sufficient symptom burden to allow meaningful improvement, while at the same time their difficulties may not have been severe enough to substantially limit their capacity to engage with and benefit from treatment.
Adolescents with moderate burden may therefore have had both sufficient scope for improvement and sufficient psychological resources to participate actively in therapeutic processes.

Previous research on adolescent depression has similarly indicated that less chronic depression, better functioning, less hopelessness, and fewer comorbid diagnoses are associated with more favorable short-term treatment outcomes (Curry et al., 2006).
text.formatted: Previous research on adolescent depression has similarly indicated that less chronic depression, better functioning, less hopelessness, and fewer comorbid diagnoses are associated with more favorable short-term treatment outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Curry et al., 2006)</ref>.

text.text: These characteristics may have been specifically suitable for engagement in the animal-assisted program.

In contrast, the elevated-burden profile showed pronounced stability: approximately 87% of adolescents initially characterized by high depressive symptoms and low mindfulness remained in this profile at T2.
Greater psychological burden may make it more difficult to engage fully with and benefit from therapeutic activities over a relatively short period.
Adolescents with greater initial burden may therefore require more intensive, longer, or differently tailored support before changes are large enough to result in a transition to another profile.

Consistent with this interpretation, previous research among adolescent psychiatric inpatients has shown that more severe clinical presentations are associated with greater symptom severity at discharge, suggesting that adolescents with higher levels of burden may require longer or more intensive treatment to achieve comparable improvement (Zambrowicz et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Consistent with this interpretation, previous research among adolescent psychiatric inpatients has shown that more severe clinical presentations are associated with greater symptom severity at discharge, suggesting that adolescents with higher levels of burden may require longer or more intensive treatment to achieve comparable improvement <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">(Zambrowicz et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Nevertheless, remaining in the same profile does not imply an absence of improvement.

Changes in depressive symptoms or mindfulness may have been too small to result in a profile transition, or participants may have improved in domains not represented in the present profiles, such as engagement, self-efficacy, social interaction, or general functioning.
Previous research has shown that improvements across different outcome domains do not necessarily occur together during adolescent mental health treatment (Krause et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Previous research has shown that improvements across different outcome domains do not necessarily occur together during adolescent mental health treatment <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Krause et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: The stability of the elevated-burden profile should therefore not be interpreted as evidence that therapy was ineffective for these adolescents.
At the other end of the spectrum, the reduced-burden profile was highly stable, with all adolescents assigned to this profile at baseline remaining in it at T2.
This indicates that adolescents who entered the program with comparatively low depressive symptoms and high mindfulness generally maintained this favorable pattern during the intervention period.
These adolescents already showed comparatively low depressive symptoms and high mindfulness, leaving less room for a transition toward a more favorable profile.

Taken together, the comparatively greater movement observed among adolescents with moderate initial burden may reflect a combination of sufficient scope for improvement and sufficient psychological resources to engage with and benefit from treatment over the five-week period.

Age and length of inpatient stay were not significantly associated with baseline profile membership or transitions, and the number of attended AAT sessions was not significantly associated with transitions.
However, the number of attended sessions captures only the quantity of exposure.

Future studies should examine therapeutic alliance, engagement with the animals, treatment expectancies, perceived relevance of the intervention, and active participation as potential predictors of profile membership and transitions.
The findings have potential implications for understanding heterogeneity among adolescents receiving inpatient treatment that includes animal-assisted group psychotherapy.
First, they suggest that adolescents participating in the same treatment context should not be assumed to follow a uniform trajectory.

Adolescents with moderate psychological burden may represent a group that is particularly likely to show favorable change over a relatively brief treatment period, whereas those with high depressive symptoms and low mindfulness may require additional preparation, greater individualization, or more intensive support.
For example, the pace and complexity of therapeutic activities could be adapted to adolescents' current capacity to engage, sustain attention, and reflect on their experiences.
Second, monitoring both symptoms and adaptive psychological resources may provide a more informative picture of change than assessing symptom reduction alone.

While symptom measures provide information about adolescents' symptom burden, assessing resources such as mindfulness may offer additional insight into their capacity to cope with psychological difficulties and engage in therapeutic processes.
Repeated assessment during treatment could help clinicians identify adolescents who remain in an elevated-burden pattern and consider whether additional or adapted support may be needed.
Several strengths should be noted.
The study examined adolescents in a naturalistic inpatient setting.
The use of LTA extended previous AAT research, which has predominantly focused on average pre-post changes or immediate session effects (Brown et al., 2020; Stefanini et al., 2015).
text.formatted: The use of LTA extended previous AAT research, which has predominantly focused on average pre-post changes or immediate session effects <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Brown et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Stefanini et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Accounting for classification uncertainty further reduced the risk of treating profile assignments as directly observed categories.
The joint consideration of depressive symptoms and mindfulness also provided information about both symptom burden and an adaptive psychological resource targeted by the intervention.
Several limitations should also be considered.
First, depressive symptoms and mindfulness were assessed in adolescents participating in AAT and inpatient treatment.

The observed profiles and transitions therefore reflect patterns occurring during multimodal inpatient treatment that included animal-assisted group psychotherapy along with other modalities and thus cannot be attributed specifically to AAT.
A randomized controlled design comparing treatment effects by modality is needed to establish such evidence.
Second, the relatively small sample size may have limited the precision and reliability of parameter estimates, particularly for transitions involving smaller profiles and for covariate analyses.
Third, the predominantly female sample (93.5%) limits generalizability, particularly to male adolescents.
A similarly female-predominant sample has been reported in comparable adolescent psychiatric AAT research (Rodrigo-Claverol et al., 2023).
text.formatted: A similarly female-predominant sample has been reported in comparable adolescent psychiatric AAT research <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Rodrigo-Claverol et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: In conclusion, adolescents participating in animal-assisted group psychotherapy within multimodal inpatient psychosomatic treatment showed three distinct depression-mindfulness profiles with different patterns of stability and change over the five-week period.

Adolescents with moderate initial burden showed the greatest movement toward a more favorable profile characterized by lower depressive symptoms and higher mindfulness, suggesting that this group may represent a particularly responsive subgroup during relatively brief treatment periods.
In contrast, the stability of the elevated-burden profile suggests that adolescents with greater symptom burden and fewer psychological resources may require more time or more individualized support.

Controlled studies with larger and more diverse samples, repeated assessments, additional indicators, and longer-term follow-up are needed to determine whether these patterns are specifically associated with AAT and to identify processes underlying more and less favorable change.
